visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to planes. The walls of a room, a sloping roof sheet and a row of solar panels are all pieces of planes. In this part we describe a plane by a point and a normal, write its vector and Cartesian equations, find the plane through three points, and meet the one-point, intercept and normal forms.

slides.heading: What you will learn

rows: write the vector and Cartesian equations of a plane through a point with a given normal
read direction ratios of the normal from an equation
find the plane through three points
write a plane in one-point, intercept and normal forms

visual.alt: Table of the four goals of Part 1: the two equations of a plane through a point with a given normal, reading the normal, the plane through three points, and the special forms of a plane.
visual.caption: Four skills for Part 1.

slides.narration: Here are the four skills for this part. All of them rest on one idea: a plane is fixed by one of its points and a direction perpendicular to it, called the normal.

slides.heading: A plane and its normal
slides.body_md: A plane is fixed by a point $\vec{a}$ on it and a normal $\vec{n}$: every $\vec{r}$ on it satisfies $(\vec{r} - \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{n} = 0$.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of the three axes with a triangular piece of a plane cutting them at A, B and C. From a point Q of the plane, a segment marked n rises at right angles to the plane: the normal vector.
visual.caption: Every line in the plane through $Q$ is perpendicular to the normal $\vec{n}$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Pick a point on the plane and a vector sticking straight out of it, the normal. For any other point of the plane, the vector joining the two points lies in the plane, so it is perpendicular to the normal. Their dot product is zero. That single condition is the equation of the plane.

slides.heading: Vector and Cartesian equations
slides.body_md: Expanding $(\vec{r} - \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{n} = 0$ gives $\vec{r} \cdot \vec{n} = d$ with $d = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{n}$; in coordinates, $ax + by + cz = d$.

rows: $a, b, c$ are direction ratios of the normal

visual.alt: Table of plane equations: vector form r dot n equals d; through a point a with normal n, r minus a dot n equals 0; Cartesian form a x plus b y plus c z equals d, whose coefficients are direction ratios of the normal; one-point form through x1, y1, z1.
visual.caption: One plane, several ways to write it.

slides.narration: Multiply out the dot product and you get r dot n equals a constant, which is the vector form. Writing r as x, y and z turns it into a x plus b y plus c z equals d, the Cartesian form. The coefficients a, b and c are direction ratios of the normal, so you can read the normal straight from the equation.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: point and normal
slides.body_md: Find the vector and Cartesian equations of the plane through $(1, -2, 3)$ with normal $2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$.

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: through 1, minus 2, 3 with normal 2, 1, minus 2, the constant a dot n is minus 6, giving r dot the normal equals minus 6, or 2x plus y minus 2z equals minus 6; the point checks.
visual.caption: Point and normal give the whole plane.

slides.narration: The constant is the dot product of the point and the normal: two minus two minus six, which is minus six. So the vector form is r dot the normal equals minus six, and the Cartesian form is two x plus y minus two z equals minus six. Substituting the point back gives minus six, as it must.

slides.heading: Quick check: from vector to Cartesian
slides.body_md: Choose the Cartesian form of the solar-panel plane.

rows: $a, b, c$ are direction ratios of the normal

visual.alt: Table of plane equations: vector form r dot n equals d; through a point a with normal n, r minus a dot n equals 0; Cartesian form a x plus b y plus c z equals d, whose coefficients are direction ratios of the normal; one-point form through x1, y1, z1.
visual.caption: One plane, several ways to write it.

slides.narration: Replace r by x i plus y j plus z k and work out the dot product.

slides.heading: A plane through three points
slides.body_md: Through $A$, $B$, $C$ (not collinear): $\vec{n} = \vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$, then use $A$.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of the axes with a triangle ABC whose corners lie on the x, y and z axes. The three corners fix one plane; two of its sides, AB and AC, are vectors lying in the plane.
visual.caption: Three points that are not collinear fix a plane; $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ is a normal (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Three points that are not on one line fix a plane. The edges A B and A C lie in the plane, so their cross product is perpendicular to both of them, and therefore perpendicular to the plane. Use it as the normal, and use the point A to find the constant.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: three points
slides.body_md: Find the plane through $A(1, 0, 1)$, $B(2, 1, 0)$ and $C(0, 3, 2)$.

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table: for A at 1, 0, 1, B at 2, 1, 0 and C at 0, 3, 2, the edges AB and AC have cross product 4 i plus 4 k, so the normal is 1, 0, 1 and the plane is x plus z equals 2; B and C both satisfy it.
visual.caption: Cross two edges, then use one point.

slides.narration: The two edges are one, one, minus one and minus one, three, one. Their cross product is four i plus four k, so a simpler normal is one, zero, one. Through A the constant is one plus one, two. The plane is x plus z equals two, and B and C both check. Notice that there is no y term.

slides.heading: Quick check: which point is on the ceiling?
slides.body_md: Substitute each position into the ceiling plane.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of the axes with a triangle ABC whose corners lie on the x, y and z axes. The three corners fix one plane; two of its sides, AB and AC, are vectors lying in the plane.
visual.caption: Three points that are not collinear fix a plane; $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ is a normal (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: A point lies on a plane exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation.

slides.heading: One-point form
slides.body_md: $a(x - x_1) + b(y - y_1) + c(z - z_1) = 0$: the plane through $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ with normal ratios $a, b, c$.

rows: $a, b, c$ are direction ratios of the normal

visual.alt: Table of plane equations: vector form r dot n equals d; through a point a with normal n, r minus a dot n equals 0; Cartesian form a x plus b y plus c z equals d, whose coefficients are direction ratios of the normal; one-point form through x1, y1, z1.
visual.caption: One plane, several ways to write it.

slides.narration: When you know one point and the direction ratios of the normal, write the one-point form: a times x minus x one, plus b times y minus y one, plus c times z minus z one, equals zero. It is the same equation as before, written so that the given point is easy to see.

slides.heading: Intercept form
slides.body_md: A plane cutting the axes at $a$, $b$, $c$: $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} + \dfrac{z}{c} = 1$.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of the plane 4x plus 3y plus 6z equals 12. It cuts the x axis at 3, the y axis at 4 and the z axis at 2, and the triangle joining these three points is the part of the plane in the first octant.
visual.caption: $4x + 3y + 6z = 12$ is $\dfrac{x}{3} + \dfrac{y}{4} + \dfrac{z}{2} = 1$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: If a plane cuts the x axis at a, the y axis at b and the z axis at c, its equation is x over a plus y over b plus z over c equals one. To find the intercepts of any plane, divide its equation so that the right side is one, then read the three denominators.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: intercepts
slides.body_md: Find the intercepts of $5x - 2y + 10z = 20$.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: dividing 5x minus 2y plus 10z equals 20 by 20 gives x over 4 plus y over minus 10 plus z over 2 equals 1, so the intercepts are 4, minus 10 and 2.
visual.caption: Make the right side $1$, then read the denominators.

slides.narration: Divide every term by twenty. Five x over twenty is x over four, minus two y over twenty is y over minus ten, and ten z over twenty is z over two. So the plane cuts the axes at four, minus ten and two. Keep the minus sign with the y intercept.

slides.heading: Normal form
slides.body_md: Divide by $|\vec{n}|$ to get $lx + my + nz = p$, with $p \ge 0$.

rows: divide the equation by $|\vec{n}|$; use $-|\vec{n}|$ if $d < 0$
$l, m, n$: direction cosines of the normal; $p$: distance from the origin

visual.alt: Table of the steps to normal form: find the length of the normal, divide by it (by its negative if the constant is negative), get l x plus m y plus n z equals p with p at least zero, where l, m, n are direction cosines of the normal and p is the distance from the origin.
visual.caption: Normal form: $p$ is never negative.

slides.narration: For the normal form, divide the whole equation by the length of the normal. The new coefficients are the direction cosines of the normal, and the right side p is the perpendicular distance of the plane from the origin. If the constant is negative, divide by minus the length instead, so that p is never negative.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: normal form
slides.body_md: Write $2x + 6y - 3z + 21 = 0$ in normal form.

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table: the plane 2x plus 6y minus 3z equals minus 21 has normal of length 7; dividing by minus 7 gives minus two sevenths x minus six sevenths y plus three sevenths z equals 3, so p is 3.
visual.caption: Divide by $-7$ because the constant is negative.

slides.narration: Move the constant across: two x plus six y minus three z equals minus twenty one. The length of the normal is seven. The right side is negative, so divide by minus seven. The plane is three units from the origin, and the direction cosines of the normal are minus two sevenths, minus six sevenths and three sevenths.

slides.heading: Quick check: read the normal
slides.body_md: Fill in the missing direction ratio of the normal.

rows: divide the equation by $|\vec{n}|$; use $-|\vec{n}|$ if $d < 0$
$l, m, n$: direction cosines of the normal; $p$: distance from the origin

visual.alt: Table of the steps to normal form: find the length of the normal, divide by it (by its negative if the constant is negative), get l x plus m y plus n z equals p with p at least zero, where l, m, n are direction cosines of the normal and p is the distance from the origin.
visual.caption: Normal form: $p$ is never negative.

slides.narration: The direction ratios of the normal are the coefficients of x, y and z.

slides.heading: Quick check: normal form of a field
slides.body_md: Choose the correct direction cosines and $p$.

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table: the plane 2x plus 6y minus 3z equals minus 21 has normal of length 7; dividing by minus 7 gives minus two sevenths x minus six sevenths y plus three sevenths z equals 3, so p is 3.
visual.caption: Divide by $-7$ because the constant is negative.

slides.narration: Remember that p in the normal form is never negative.

slides.heading: Special planes
slides.body_md: Some planes can be recognised at a glance.

visual.alt: Table of special planes: through the origin the constant is 0; parallel to the yz plane it is x equals k; parallel to the x axis there is no x term; parallel to a given plane it has the same left side.
visual.caption: Spot these at a glance.

slides.narration: A few planes are worth recognising at once. A plane through the origin has constant zero. A plane parallel to the y z plane is x equals a constant. If the x term is missing, the plane is parallel to the x axis. And a plane parallel to a given plane keeps the same left side and changes only the constant.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: coefficients $a, b, c$ of $ax + by + cz = d$

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the normal comes from the coefficients; the vector form is r dot n equals a dot n; through three points the normal is AB cross AC; intercept form x over a plus y over b plus z over c equals 1; normal form with p at least zero.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up. The coefficients of x, y and z give the normal. Through a point with a given normal, r dot n equals a dot n. Through three points, cross two edges for the normal. Intercept form has right side one, and normal form has a non-negative p, the distance from the origin.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the normal before the equation
Substitute every given point into your answer
Divide so the right side is $1$ for intercepts

nodes.label: Show the normal before the equation
Check every given point in your answer
Right side 1 for intercept form
p must not be negative in normal form

visual.alt: Exam-tip flow: show the normal before writing the equation; substitute every given point into your answer; make the right side 1 for intercept form; keep p non-negative in normal form.
visual.caption: Habits that protect marks.

slides.narration: In the examination, write the normal first: it earns a mark on its own. Substitute each given point into your final equation; it takes seconds and catches sign slips. For intercepts, make the right side one before reading. And in normal form, check that p is not negative.

decks.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry: Planes — Part 2: Distances, meeting points and angles
goals: Find the distance of a point from a plane, with the foot and image of the point
Find the distance between parallel planes
Find where a line meets a plane, or show that it is parallel to the plane
Find the angle between two planes and between a line and a plane

slides.heading: Three-Dimensional Geometry: Planes, Part 2
slides.body_md: How far is a point from a plane, where does a line pierce it, and at what angle?

nodes.label: Distance of a point from a plane
Parallel planes
Where a line meets a plane
Angles

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the distance of a point from a plane, the distance between parallel planes, the point where a line meets a plane, and the angles between two planes and between a line and a plane.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: In this part we measure. How far is a drone from a glass roof? Where does a cable pass through a wall? At what angle do two roof sheets meet, or does a ski cable cross a hillside? Each question has a short formula built on the normal of the plane.

slides.heading: What you will learn
bullets: **Distance** of a point from a plane; **foot** and **image**
**Angles** between planes, and between a line and a plane

rows: find the distance of a point from a plane, and the foot and image
find the distance between parallel planes
find where a line meets a plane, or show it is parallel
find the angle between two planes and between a line and a plane

visual.alt: Table of the four goals of Part 2: distance of a point from a plane with the foot and image, distance between parallel planes, the meeting point of a line and a plane, and the two kinds of angle.
visual.caption: Four skills for Part 2.

slides.narration: Here are the four skills for Part 2. Keep the normal of the plane in mind throughout; almost every formula uses it.

slides.heading: Distance of a point from a plane
slides.body_md: The shortest path from $P$ to the plane runs along the normal and meets it at the foot $F$.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of a triangular piece of a plane with a point P outside it. A dashed segment from P meets the plane at F at right angles; its length PF is the distance of P from the plane.
visual.caption: $PF$ runs along the normal; $PF = \dfrac{|\vec{n} \cdot \vec{p} - d|}{|\vec{n}|}$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: The shortest way from a point to a plane is straight along the normal. The perpendicular meets the plane at the foot F, and the length P F is the distance. Projecting the vector from any point of the plane to P onto the normal gives a neat formula for this length.

slides.heading: Distance formulas
slides.body_md: Substitute the point, subtract the constant, divide by the length of the normal.

rows: Point $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ from $ax + by + cz = d$
Parallel planes $ax + by + cz = d_1, d_2$

visual.alt: Table of distance formulas: a point from a plane is the absolute value of a x1 plus b y1 plus c z1 minus d over the length of the normal; the vector version; the origin is the absolute value of d over the length of the normal; parallel planes with the same coefficients are the absolute difference of the constants over the length of the normal.
visual.caption: Substitute, subtract, divide by $|\vec{n}|$.

slides.narration: To find the distance of a point from a x plus b y plus c z equals d, substitute the point into the left side, subtract d, take the modulus and divide by the length of the normal. For the origin this is just the modulus of d over the length. For parallel planes, first make the coefficients identical, then use the difference of the constants.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a point and a plane
slides.body_md: Find the distance of $(2, -3, 4)$ from $6x + 2y - 3z = 8$.

visual.alt: Worked example 5 table: substituting 2, minus 3, 4 into 6x plus 2y minus 3z minus 8 gives minus 14; the normal has length 7; the distance is 2.
visual.caption: The modulus makes the distance positive.

slides.narration: Substitute the point: twelve minus six minus twelve, minus eight, gives minus fourteen. The length of the normal is seven. The modulus of minus fourteen over seven is two, so the point is two units from the plane.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: parallel planes
slides.body_md: Find the distance between $x - 2y + 2z = 4$ and $2x - 4y + 4z = -10$.

visual.alt: Worked example 6 table: rewrite 2x minus 4y plus 4z equals minus 10 as x minus 2y plus 2z equals minus 5; the normal has length 3; the gap is the absolute value of 4 minus minus 5, over 3, which is 3; the point 4, 0, 0 of the first plane is also 3 from the second.
visual.caption: Make the left sides identical first.

slides.narration: The second plane has every coefficient doubled, so divide it by two first: x minus two y plus two z equals minus five. Now the left sides match. The difference of the constants is nine, and the length of the normal is three, so the planes are three units apart.

slides.heading: Quick check: double glazing
slides.body_md: Choose the gap between the two panes.

rows: Point $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ from $ax + by + cz = d$
Parallel planes $ax + by + cz = d_1, d_2$

visual.alt: Table of distance formulas: a point from a plane is the absolute value of a x1 plus b y1 plus c z1 minus d over the length of the normal; the vector version; the origin is the absolute value of d over the length of the normal; parallel planes with the same coefficients are the absolute difference of the constants over the length of the normal.
visual.caption: Substitute, subtract, divide by $|\vec{n}|$.

slides.narration: Before using the parallel-planes formula, make the coefficients identical.

slides.heading: Foot and image of a point
slides.body_md: The foot $F$ is where the normal through $P$ meets the plane; the image is $P' = 2F - P$.

visual.alt: The same plane with a point P above it, the foot F on the plane, and the image P prime on the other side, so that F is the midpoint of P and P prime along the normal.
visual.caption: Image of $P$: $P' = 2F - P$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: To find the foot, write the line through P along the normal, and find where it meets the plane. The image of P in the plane is just as far on the other side, so the foot is the midpoint of P and its image. That gives the image as two F minus P.

slides.heading: Quick check: a spotlight and a backdrop
slides.body_md: Find the distance of the spotlight from the backdrop.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of a triangular piece of a plane with a point P outside it. A dashed segment from P meets the plane at F at right angles; its length PF is the distance of P from the plane.
visual.caption: $PF$ runs along the normal; $PF = \dfrac{|\vec{n} \cdot \vec{p} - d|}{|\vec{n}|}$ (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: Substitute, subtract, take the modulus and divide by the length of the normal.

slides.heading: Where a line meets a plane
slides.body_md: Write a general point of the line and substitute it into the plane.

visual.alt: A sketch of a triangular piece of a plane and a straight line passing through it at the point M. The line enters from above and leaves below the plane.
visual.caption: A line that is not parallel to a plane meets it at exactly one point (sketch, not to scale).

slides.narration: A line that is not parallel to a plane passes through it at exactly one point. Write a general point of the line in terms of lambda, substitute it into the equation of the plane, and solve for lambda. Putting lambda back gives the meeting point.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a line meets a plane
slides.body_md: Find where $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{1} = \dfrac{z - 2}{-1}$ meets $x + y + z = 8$.

visual.alt: Worked example 7 table: the general point 1 plus 2 lambda, minus 1 plus lambda, 2 minus lambda substituted in x plus y plus z equals 8 gives 2 plus 2 lambda equals 8, so lambda is 3 and the point is 7, 2, minus 1.
visual.caption: General point, substitute, solve, check.

slides.narration: A general point of the line is one plus two lambda, minus one plus lambda, two minus lambda. Adding the coordinates gives two plus two lambda, which must be eight, so lambda is three. The meeting point is seven, two, minus one, and its coordinates do add up to eight.

slides.heading: Meets, parallel, or lies in?
slides.body_md: Test $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n}$ first, then one point of the line.

nodes.label: Is $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n} = 0$?
No: the line meets the plane at one point
Yes: the line is parallel to the plane
A point of the line satisfies the plane: the line lies in it
It does not: parallel, never meeting

visual.alt: Decision flow for a line and a plane: if b dot n is not zero, the line meets the plane at one point; if it is zero, the line is parallel, and it lies in the plane if one of its points satisfies the plane equation, otherwise it never meets it.
visual.caption: Meets, parallel, or lies in?

slides.narration: If the direction of the line is not perpendicular to the normal, the line meets the plane at one point. If the direction is perpendicular to the normal, the line is parallel to the plane. Then test one point of the line: if it satisfies the plane, the whole line lies in it; otherwise the line never meets the plane.

slides.heading: Quick check: a handrail parallel to a floor
slides.body_md: Find $k$ so that the handrail is parallel to the floor.

nodes.label: Is $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n} = 0$?
No: the line meets the plane at one point
Yes: the line is parallel to the plane
A point of the line satisfies the plane: the line lies in it
It does not: parallel, never meeting

visual.alt: Decision flow for a line and a plane: if b dot n is not zero, the line meets the plane at one point; if it is zero, the line is parallel, and it lies in the plane if one of its points satisfies the plane equation, otherwise it never meets it.
visual.caption: Meets, parallel, or lies in?

slides.narration: Parallel to the plane means perpendicular to its normal.

slides.heading: Angles with planes
slides.body_md: Planes: angle between the normals. Line and plane: complement of the angle with the normal, so use sine.

rows: Line with direction $\vec{b}$ and plane with normal $\vec{n}$

visual.alt: Table of angle formulas: the angle between planes uses the cosine of the angle between normals; the angle between a line and a plane uses the sine with the direction and the normal; perpendicular planes have perpendicular normals; a line parallel to a plane is perpendicular to the normal; a line perpendicular to a plane is parallel to the normal.
visual.caption: Planes: cosine. Line and plane: sine.

slides.narration: The angle between two planes is the angle between their normals, so use the cosine formula with the two normals. For a line and a plane, the angle with the plane is ninety degrees minus the angle with the normal, so the same expression gives the sine of the angle instead of the cosine.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: the angle between two planes
slides.body_md: Find the angle between $2x - y + z = 6$ and $x + y + 2z = 7$.

visual.alt: Worked example 8 table: the planes 2x minus y plus z equals 6 and x plus y plus 2z equals 7 have normals with dot product 3 and lengths root 6 each, so the cosine is one half and the angle is 60 degrees.
visual.caption: The angle between planes is the angle between normals.

slides.narration: The normals are two, minus one, one and one, one, two. Their dot product is three and each has length root six. So the cosine of the angle is three over six, a half, and the planes meet at sixty degrees.

slides.heading: Worked example 9: a line and a plane
slides.body_md: Find the angle between a line with direction ratios $1, 1, 2$ and the plane $2x - y + z = 4$.

visual.alt: Worked example 9 table: a line with direction 1, 1, 2 and the plane 2x minus y plus z equals 4 give dot product 3 and lengths root 6, so the sine of the angle is one half and the angle is 30 degrees.
visual.caption: Sine, not cosine, for a line and a plane.

slides.narration: The direction of the line and the normal have dot product three and lengths root six each. For a line and a plane this gives the sine: a half. So the line makes thirty degrees with the plane. Using cosine here would wrongly give sixty degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false
slides.body_md: A line perpendicular to a plane and the normal of the plane.

rows: Line with direction $\vec{b}$ and plane with normal $\vec{n}$

visual.alt: Table of angle formulas: the angle between planes uses the cosine of the angle between normals; the angle between a line and a plane uses the sine with the direction and the normal; perpendicular planes have perpendicular normals; a line parallel to a plane is perpendicular to the normal; a line perpendicular to a plane is parallel to the normal.
visual.caption: Planes: cosine. Line and plane: sine.

slides.narration: Look at the last row of the angle table.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: Foot along the normal; image $2F - P$
Meeting point: general point into the plane
Planes: cosine; line and plane: sine

rows: same $a, b, c$ first, then $\dfrac{|d_1 - d_2|}{|\vec{n}|}$
planes: cosine of normals; line and plane: sine

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: the distance formula; parallel planes need the same coefficients first; the foot lies along the normal and the image is 2F minus P; a line meets a plane by substituting a general point; the angle between planes uses cosine, a line and a plane uses sine.
visual.caption: Part 2 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up. The distance of a point from a plane comes from substituting, subtracting and dividing by the length of the normal. For parallel planes, equalise the coefficients first. The foot lies along the normal, and the image is two F minus P. A line meets a plane where its general point satisfies the equation. And for angles, use cosine for two planes and sine for a line and a plane.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Equalise coefficients before the parallel-planes formula
Keep the modulus in every distance
Sine for a line and a plane

nodes.label: Equalise coefficients before the parallel-planes formula
Keep the modulus in every distance
Line and plane: sine, not cosine
Substitute the meeting point back

visual.alt: Exam-tip flow: make the coefficients equal before using the parallel-planes formula; keep the modulus in every distance; use sine for a line and a plane; substitute the meeting point back into the plane.
visual.caption: Most lost marks come from these four slips.

slides.narration: In the examination, never use the parallel-planes formula until the coefficients match. Keep the modulus, because a distance is never negative. Use sine for the angle between a line and a plane. And substitute any meeting point back into the plane to check it.

notes.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry: Planes — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Vector and Cartesian equations of a plane
sections.body_md:
- Through the point $\vec{a}$ with normal $\vec{n}$: $(\vec{r} - \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{n} = 0$, i.e. $\vec{r} \cdot \vec{n} = d$ with $d = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{n}$.
- Cartesian form $ax + by + cz = d$: the coefficients $a, b, c$ are direction ratios of the normal.
- A point lies on the plane exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation.
- Parallel planes have proportional normals; a plane through the origin has $d = 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: A vector perpendicular to every line lying in the plane.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of the three axes with a triangular piece of a plane cutting them at A, B and C. From a point Q of the plane, a segment marked n rises at right angles to the plane: the normal vector.
visual.caption: Every line in the plane through $Q$ is perpendicular to the normal $\vec{n}$ (sketch, not to scale).

sections.heading: 2. Plane through three points
sections.body_md:
- Through non-collinear $A$, $B$, $C$: $\vec{n} = \vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$, and $\vec{r} \cdot \vec{n} = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{n}$.
- Equivalently $(\vec{r} - \vec{a}) \cdot [(\vec{b} - \vec{a}) \times (\vec{c} - \vec{a})] = 0$.
- Always substitute all three points into the answer.

key_terms.definition_md: Points not on one line; three such points fix exactly one plane.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of the axes with a triangle ABC whose corners lie on the x, y and z axes. The three corners fix one plane; two of its sides, AB and AC, are vectors lying in the plane.
visual.caption: Three points that are not collinear fix a plane; $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$ is a normal (sketch, not to scale).

visuals.alt: Worked example 2 table: for A at 1, 0, 1, B at 2, 1, 0 and C at 0, 3, 2, the edges AB and AC have cross product 4 i plus 4 k, so the normal is 1, 0, 1 and the plane is x plus z equals 2; B and C both satisfy it.
visuals.caption: Cross two edges, then use one point.

sections.heading: 3. One-point, intercept and normal forms
sections.body_md:
- **One-point form:** $a(x - x_1) + b(y - y_1) + c(z - z_1) = 0$.
- **Intercept form:** $\dfrac{x}{a} + \dfrac{y}{b} + \dfrac{z}{c} = 1$ for intercepts $a$, $b$, $c$ (divide so the right side is $1$).
- **Normal form:** $lx + my + nz = p$ (vector form $\vec{r} \cdot \hat{n} = p$), where $l, m, n$ are direction cosines of the normal and $p \ge 0$ is the distance from the origin. Divide by $|\vec{n}|$, or by $-|\vec{n}|$ if the constant is negative.

key_terms.definition_md: The coordinate at which a plane cuts an axis.
An equation of the plane with unit normal and non-negative constant.

visual.alt: An oblique sketch of the plane 4x plus 3y plus 6z equals 12. It cuts the x axis at 3, the y axis at 4 and the z axis at 2, and the triangle joining these three points is the part of the plane in the first octant.
visual.caption: $4x + 3y + 6z = 12$ is $\dfrac{x}{3} + \dfrac{y}{4} + \dfrac{z}{2} = 1$ (sketch, not to scale).

visuals.alt: Worked example 3 table: dividing 5x minus 2y plus 10z equals 20 by 20 gives x over 4 plus y over minus 10 plus z over 2 equals 1, so the intercepts are 4, minus 10 and 2.
visuals.caption: Make the right side $1$, then read the denominators.

rows: divide the equation by $|\vec{n}|$; use $-|\vec{n}|$ if $d < 0$
$l, m, n$: direction cosines of the normal; $p$: distance from the origin

visuals.alt: Table of the steps to normal form: find the length of the normal, divide by it (by its negative if the constant is negative), get l x plus m y plus n z equals p with p at least zero, where l, m, n are direction cosines of the normal and p is the distance from the origin.
visuals.caption: Normal form: $p$ is never negative.

visuals.alt: Worked example 4 table: the plane 2x plus 6y minus 3z equals minus 21 has normal of length 7; dividing by minus 7 gives minus two sevenths x minus six sevenths y plus three sevenths z equals 3, so p is 3.
visuals.caption: Divide by $-7$ because the constant is negative.

visuals.caption: Spot these at a glance.

sections.heading: 4. Distance of a point from a plane
sections.body_md:
- From $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ to $ax + by + cz = d$: $\dfrac{|ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 - d|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$; vector form $\dfrac{|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{n} - d|}{|\vec{n}|}$.
- **Parallel planes** $ax + by + cz = d_1$ and $ax + by + cz = d_2$ (same coefficients): $\dfrac{|d_1 - d_2|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$.
- **Foot** of the perpendicular from $P$: where the line through $P$ along $\vec{n}$ meets the plane. **Image**: $2F - P$.

key_terms.definition_md: The point of the plane nearest to the given point.

formulas.latex: d = \dfrac{|ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 - d|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}
formulas.label: Point to plane

visuals.caption: Substitute, subtract, divide by $|\vec{n}|$.

visuals.caption: Image of $P$: $P' = 2F - P$ (sketch, not to scale).

sections.heading: 5. A line and a plane: meeting point, parallel, lying in
sections.body_md:
- To find where $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$ meets $\vec{r} \cdot \vec{n} = d$: substitute the general point, solve for $\lambda$, put it back, and check.
- If $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n} = 0$ the line is parallel to the plane: it lies in the plane if one of its points satisfies the equation, and never meets it otherwise.
- If $\vec{b} \parallel \vec{n}$ the line is perpendicular to the plane.

key_terms.definition_md: A line whose direction is perpendicular to the normal: $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n} = 0$.

visual.alt: A sketch of a triangular piece of a plane and a straight line passing through it at the point M. The line enters from above and leaves below the plane.
visual.caption: A line that is not parallel to a plane meets it at exactly one point (sketch, not to scale).

nodes.label: Write a general point of the line
Substitute it into the plane
Solve for $\lambda$
Put $\lambda$ back: the meeting point
Check it in the plane

visuals.alt: Flow for the meeting point of a line and a plane: write a general point of the line, substitute it into the plane, solve for lambda, put lambda back to get the point, and check it in the plane.
visuals.caption: Five steps to the meeting point.

visuals.alt: Worked example 7 table: the general point 1 plus 2 lambda, minus 1 plus lambda, 2 minus lambda substituted in x plus y plus z equals 8 gives 2 plus 2 lambda equals 8, so lambda is 3 and the point is 7, 2, minus 1.
visuals.caption: General point, substitute, solve, check.

nodes.label: Is $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n} = 0$?
No: the line meets the plane at one point
Yes: the line is parallel to the plane
A point of the line satisfies the plane: the line lies in it
It does not: parallel, never meeting

visuals.alt: Decision flow for a line and a plane: if b dot n is not zero, the line meets the plane at one point; if it is zero, the line is parallel, and it lies in the plane if one of its points satisfies the plane equation, otherwise it never meets it.
visuals.caption: Meets, parallel, or lies in?

sections.heading: 6. Angles
sections.body_md:
- **Between two planes:** $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|\vec{n}_1 \cdot \vec{n}_2|}{|\vec{n}_1|\,|\vec{n}_2|}$. Perpendicular planes: $a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2 = 0$; parallel planes: proportional normals.
- **Between a line and a plane:** $\sin\phi = \dfrac{|\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n}|}{|\vec{b}|\,|\vec{n}|}$ (the complement of the angle with the normal).

rows: Line with direction $\vec{b}$ and plane with normal $\vec{n}$

visual.alt: Table of angle formulas: the angle between planes uses the cosine of the angle between normals; the angle between a line and a plane uses the sine with the direction and the normal; perpendicular planes have perpendicular normals; a line parallel to a plane is perpendicular to the normal; a line perpendicular to a plane is parallel to the normal.
visual.caption: Planes: cosine. Line and plane: sine.

visuals.alt: Worked example 8 table: the planes 2x minus y plus z equals 6 and x plus y plus 2z equals 7 have normals with dot product 3 and lengths root 6 each, so the cosine is one half and the angle is 60 degrees.
visuals.caption: The angle between planes is the angle between normals.

visuals.alt: Worked example 9 table: a line with direction 1, 1, 2 and the plane 2x minus y plus z equals 4 give dot product 3 and lengths root 6, so the sine of the angle is one half and the angle is 30 degrees.
visuals.caption: Sine, not cosine, for a line and a plane.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are awarded**
- *Plane through a point (2 marks):* normal and constant, then the equation.
- *Plane through three points (3 marks):* two edge vectors, normal by cross product, equation with a check.
- *Distance (2–3 marks):* substitution, length of the normal, answer with modulus.
- *Meeting point (3 marks):* general point, $\lambda$, point and check.
- *Angle (2 marks):* dot product and lengths, then the angle.

**Common mistakes**
- Using the parallel-planes formula before making the coefficients equal.
- Dropping the modulus, so that a distance comes out negative.
- Using cosine for the angle between a line and a plane.
- A negative $p$ in normal form.
- Reading the constant $d$ as part of the normal.

questions.stem_md: A glass wall of an imagined airport lounge passes through the point $(2, -1, 3)$ and has normal $4\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. Its Cartesian equation is
questions.solution_md: $4(x - 2) - (y + 1) + 2(z - 3) = 0$ gives $4x - y + 2z = 8 + 1 + 6 = 15$. Option (c) uses the point as the normal.

questions.stem_md: The tilted surface of a skateboard ramp lies in the plane $3x - 5y + z = 7$. Direction ratios of a line perpendicular to the ramp surface are
questions.solution_md: In $ax + by + cz = d$ the coefficients $a, b, c$ are direction ratios of the normal. The constant $7$ fixes the position of the plane, not its direction.

questions.stem_md: An engineer records the plane of a row of solar panels as $\vec{r} \cdot (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}) = 6$. The same plane in Cartesian form is
questions.solution_md: Put $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$: the dot product is $x + 2y - 2z$, so the plane is $x + 2y - 2z = 6$.

questions.stem_md: Three anchor bolts of a tilted canopy over an imagined bus stop sit at $A(1, 1, 0)$, $B(3, 0, 1)$ and $C(0, 2, 2)$. The plane of the canopy is
questions.solution_md: $\vec{AB} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{AC} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$; $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = -3\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, so a normal is $3, 5, -1$ and $d = 3 + 5 - 0 = 8$. Check $C$: $0 + 10 - 2 = 8$.

questions.stem_md: Which of these positions for a smoke detector lies on the ceiling plane $2x - 3y + z = 4$ of an imagined hall?
questions.solution_md: Substitute: $(1, -1, -1)$ gives $2 + 3 - 1 = 4$. The others give $2$, $-4$ and $3$.

questions.stem_md: A decorative screen must pass through the origin and be parallel to a partition wall $2x + 3y - z = 5$. The plane of the screen is
questions.solution_md: Parallel planes share the normal $2, 3, -1$; through the origin the constant is $0$.

questions.stem_md: A sloping roof sheet of an imagined cowshed lies in the plane $4x - 3y + 6z = 12$. Its intercepts on the $x$-, $y$- and $z$-axes are
questions.solution_md: Divide by $12$: $\dfrac{x}{3} + \dfrac{y}{-4} + \dfrac{z}{2} = 1$, so the intercepts are $3$, $-4$ and $2$. Option (d) lists the coefficients.

questions.stem_md: A triangular sail in a model boat lies in a plane that cuts the axes at $2$, $-3$ and $4$ units from the origin. The plane of the sail is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{y}{-3} + \dfrac{z}{4} = 1$; multiply by $12$: $6x - 4y + 3z = 12$.

questions.stem_md: After writing the plane $2x - y + 2z = 9$ of a theatre backdrop in normal form, a student reads off its perpendicular distance from the origin. That distance is
questions.solution_md: $|\vec{n}| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$; dividing gives $\dfrac23x - \dfrac13y + \dfrac23z = 3$, so $p = 3$.

questions.stem_md: A surveyor writes the plane $6x + 2y - 3z = 14$ of a sloping field in normal form $lx + my + nz = p$. Which pair of direction cosines and $p$ is correct?
questions.solution_md: $|\vec{n}| = 7$; divide by $7$: $\dfrac67x + \dfrac27y - \dfrac37z = 2$. In normal form $p \ge 0$, so option (c) is not allowed even though it describes the same plane.

questions.stem_md: A laser level is set up along the line joining $(1, 1, 1)$ and $(3, -1, 2)$. A partition must pass through $(-1, 2, 0)$ and be perpendicular to the laser beam. Its equation is
questions.solution_md: The beam has direction $2, -2, 1$, which is the normal of the partition: $2(x + 1) - 2(y - 2) + 1(z - 0) = 0$, i.e. $2x - 2y + z = -6$.

questions.stem_md: A signboard plane makes equal intercepts on the three axes and passes through the point $(2, 3, -1)$. Its equation is
questions.solution_md: Equal intercepts $a$: $x + y + z = a$. Through $(2, 3, -1)$: $a = 2 + 3 - 1 = 4$.

questions.stem_md: A drone hovers at $(3, -1, 2)$ near the sloping glass roof $2x - 2y + z = 5$ of an imagined mall (units in metres). Its distance from the roof is
questions.solution_md: $d = \dfrac{|6 + 2 + 2 - 5|}{\sqrt{4 + 4 + 1}} = \dfrac53$ m. Option (b) forgets to divide by $|\vec{n}| = 3$.

A student finds the gap between the parallel glass panes $2x + y - 2z = 3$ and $4x + 2y - 4z = 9$ of a double-glazed window. The correct gap is
questions.solution_md: First make the coefficients equal: the second pane is $2x + y - 2z = \dfrac92$. Gap $= \dfrac{|3 - \frac92|}{3} = \dfrac12$. Option (d) comes from using $|3 - 9|$ without rewriting.

questions.stem_md: A support rod is fixed from the origin straight onto the panel $2x + 3y + 6z = 49$, meeting it at right angles. The rod touches the panel at
questions.solution_md: The rod lies along the normal: points $(2t, 3t, 6t)$. In the plane, $49t = 49$, so $t = 1$ and the foot is $(2, 3, 6)$.

questions.stem_md: A straight water jet follows $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{3} = \dfrac{z}{-1}$ and hits a screen in the plane $x + y + z = 4$. The jet hits the screen at
questions.solution_md: General point $(1 + 2\lambda, -1 + 3\lambda, -\lambda)$; in the plane $4\lambda = 4$, so $\lambda = 1$ and the point is $(3, 2, -1)$.

questions.stem_md: Two flaps of a folding table lie in the planes $x + 2y + 2z = 5$ and $2x - y + 2z = 1$. The angle between the flaps is
questions.solution_md: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|2 - 2 + 4|}{3 \times 3} = \dfrac49$. The angle between planes is the angle between their normals.

questions.stem_md: A ski-lift cable has direction ratios $2, 1, 2$ and passes over a hillside in the plane $x - 4y + 8z = 11$. The angle $\phi$ between the cable and the hillside is
questions.solution_md: For a line and a plane, $\sin\phi = \dfrac{|\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n}|}{|\vec{b}|\,|\vec{n}|} = \dfrac{|2 - 4 + 16|}{3 \times 9} = \dfrac{14}{27}$. Option (d) is the angle between the cable and the normal.

questions.stem_md: For which $k$ are the planes $2x - y + kz = 3$ and $x + 3y + 2z = 1$ of two crossing walls perpendicular?
questions.solution_md: Perpendicular planes have perpendicular normals: $2 - 3 + 2k = 0$, so $k = \dfrac12$.

questions.stem_md: A handrail with direction ratios $3, -2, k$ must run parallel to the sloping floor $x + 2y - z = 7$. Then $k$ equals
questions.solution_md: A line parallel to a plane is perpendicular to its normal: $3 - 4 - k = 0$, so $k = -1$.

questions.stem_md: A conveyor belt runs along $\vec{r} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \lambda(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})$ and a loading deck lies in the plane $x - y - z = 2$. Which statement is true?

options.text_md: The belt is perpendicular to the deck
The belt lies in the plane of the deck
The belt is parallel to the deck but never meets it
The belt meets the deck at exactly one point

questions.solution_md: $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n} = 2 - 1 - 1 = 0$, so the belt is parallel to the plane; and its point $(1, -1, 0)$ satisfies $1 + 1 - 0 = 2$. A parallel line with one point in the plane lies in it.

questions.stem_md: A lift shaft follows $\dfrac{x - 2}{3} = \dfrac{y + 1}{-6} = \dfrac{z}{2}$ and a landing floor lies in the plane $3x - 6y + 2z = 0$. The angle between the shaft and the floor is
questions.solution_md: The direction ratios of the shaft equal those of the floor's normal, so the shaft is perpendicular to the floor: $\sin\phi = 1$.

questions.stem_md: A no-fly sheet for drones is the plane through the point with position vector $2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, perpendicular to $3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - \hat{k}$. Its vector equation is
questions.solution_md: $(\vec{r} - \vec{a}) \cdot \vec{n} = 0$ gives $\vec{r} \cdot \vec{n} = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{n} = 6 - 4 - 1 = 1$.

questions.stem_md: A weather balloon is at the point with position vector $\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$, and a radar sheet is the plane $\vec{r} \cdot (2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}) = 4$. The balloon's distance from the sheet is
A stage curtain hangs in a plane parallel to the $yz$-plane, $5$ units in front of it along the positive $x$-axis. Its equation is
questions.solution_md: A plane parallel to the $yz$-plane has normal along the $x$-axis, so its equation is $x = $ constant; here $x = 5$.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the plane $5x - 2y + z = 0$ of a model's mirror passes through the origin.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the plane $\dfrac{x}{4} + \dfrac{y}{-2} + \dfrac{z}{5} = 1$ cuts the $y$-axis at $(0, 2, 0)$.
questions.solution_md: False. Put $x = z = 0$: $\dfrac{y}{-2} = 1$, so $y = -2$; the plane cuts the $y$-axis at $(0, -2, 0)$.

questions.stem_md: True or false: if a line is perpendicular to a plane, its direction ratios are proportional to the direction ratios of the plane's normal.
questions.solution_md: True: a line perpendicular to a plane is parallel to its normal, so their direction ratios are proportional.

questions.stem_md: In the normal form $lx + my + nz = p$ of a plane, $p$ is the perpendicular ____ of the plane from the origin.

questions.stem_md: The plane $4x - y + 7z = 9$ has a normal with direction ratios $4$, $-1$ and ____.

questions.stem_md: A line is parallel to a plane when the direction of the line is ____ to the normal of the plane.

questions.stem_md: The lid of an imagined storage chest, when open, lies in the plane through $(-1, 4, 2)$ with normal $2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$. Write the vector and Cartesian equations of this plane.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: Reduce the plane $2x - 6y + 3z = 14$ of an imagined ramp to normal form. State the direction cosines of its normal and its distance from the origin.

answer.model_answer_md:

Direction cosines $\dfrac27, -\dfrac67, \dfrac37$; distance from the origin $p = 2$.

questions.stem_md: Write the plane $3x + 4y - 6z = 24$ of a gable wall in intercept form and state the three intercepts.

questions.stem_md: Two parallel steel plates in a press lie in $\vec{r} \cdot (2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}) = 5$ and $\vec{r} \cdot (-4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}) = 8$. Find the distance between the plates.

questions.stem_md: A ski-jump track runs along $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} + \hat{j})$ above a slope in the plane $x + z = 6$. Find the angle between the track and the slope.

questions.stem_md: Three corners of an imagined triangular skylight are $P(2, 1, 0)$, $Q(3, -2, 1)$ and $R(1, 0, 4)$. Find the vector and Cartesian equations of the plane of the skylight.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\vec{PQ} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{PR} = -\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$.

$\vec{PQ} \times \vec{PR} = -11\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}$, so take $\vec{n} = 11\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $d = 22 + 5 + 0 = 27$.

$\vec{r} \cdot (11\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}) = 27$, i.e. $11x + 5y + 4z = 27$. Check $R$: $11 + 0 + 16 = 27$.

questions.stem_md: A plane meets the axes at $A$, $B$ and $C$, and the centroid of triangle $ABC$ is $(2, -1, 3)$. Find the equation of the plane.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $A(a, 0, 0)$, $B(0, b, 0)$, $C(0, 0, c)$. The centroid is $\left(\dfrac a3, \dfrac b3, \dfrac c3\right) = (2, -1, 3)$, so $a = 6$, $b = -3$, $c = 9$.

Intercept form: $\dfrac{x}{6} + \dfrac{y}{-3} + \dfrac{z}{9} = 1$; multiply by $18$: $3x - 6y + 2z = 18$.

questions.stem_md: Write the plane $6x - 2y + 9z + 22 = 0$ of an imagined embankment in normal form, in both Cartesian and vector forms, and state its distance from the origin.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: A camera at $P(5, 2, -1)$ is to be wired straight to the nearest point of a wall $x - 2y + 2z = -10$. Find the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the wall and the length of wire needed.

The perpendicular is $\vec{r} = (5, 2, -1) + t(1, -2, 2)$. In the plane: $(5 + t) - 2(2 - 2t) + 2(-1 + 2t) = -10 \Rightarrow -1 + 9t = -10 \Rightarrow t = -1$.

Foot $(4, 4, -3)$; length $\sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$.

questions.stem_md: A partition must pass through $(1, 1, -1)$ and be perpendicular to both walls $x + 2y + 3z = 7$ and $2x - 3y + 4z = 0$ of an imagined studio. Find the equation of the partition.

answer.model_answer_md:
Its normal is perpendicular to both normals: $(1, 2, 3) \times (2, -3, 4) = (8 + 9)\hat{i} - (4 - 6)\hat{j} + (-3 - 4)\hat{k} = 17\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}$.

$d = 17 + 2 + 7 = 26$: $17x + 2y - 7z = 26$.

questions.stem_md: A laser runs along $\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y}{2} = \dfrac{z}{3}$ from the origin, and a target sits at $(2, -1, 1)$. Find the plane that contains both the laser line and the target.

questions.stem_md:
A triangular shade sail in an imagined school courtyard is tied to points $A(2, 0, 0)$, $B(0, -3, 0)$ and $C(0, 0, 6)$ on the three axes.

(a) Write the equation of the plane of the sail in intercept form and in the form $ax + by + cz = d$. [2]

(b) Using $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}$, confirm the direction ratios of its normal. [1]

(c) Find the perpendicular distance of the origin from the sail. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{y}{-3} + \dfrac{z}{6} = 1$; multiplying by $6$: $3x - 2y + z = 6$.

**(b)** $\vec{AB} = -2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j}$, $\vec{AC} = -2\hat{i} + 6\hat{k}$; $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = -18\hat{i} + 12\hat{j} - 6\hat{k} = -6(3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k})$, so the normal has ratios $3, -2, 1$.

**(c)** $p = \dfrac{|0 - 6|}{\sqrt{9 + 4 + 1}} = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{14}}$.

questions.solution_md: Intercept form; cross product; distance from the origin.

questions.stem_md:
A light source at $P(4, 3, -1)$ shines on a flat mirror lying in the plane $2x + y - 2z = 4$.

(a) Find the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the mirror. [3]

(b) Find the distance of $P$ from the mirror. [1]

(c) Find the image of $P$ in the mirror. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The perpendicular from $P$: $(4 + 2t, 3 + t, -1 - 2t)$. In the plane: $2(4 + 2t) + (3 + t) - 2(-1 - 2t) = 13 + 9t = 4 \Rightarrow t = -1$.

Foot $F(2, 2, 1)$.

**(b)** $PF = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$ (check: $\dfrac{|8 + 3 + 2 - 4|}{3} = 3$).

**(c)** $F$ is the midpoint of $P$ and its image $P'$: $P' = 2F - P = (0, 1, 3)$.

questions.solution_md: Line along the normal; distance; midpoint for the image.

questions.stem_md:
A cable car moves in a straight line from station $A(1, 2, -1)$ towards $B(3, 1, 1)$ and would reach a hillside in the plane $x + 2y + 3z = 14$.

(a) Find the point where the line $AB$ meets the hillside. [3]

(b) Find the angle between the line $AB$ and the hillside. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Direction $\vec{AB} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$; general point $(1 + 2\lambda, 2 - \lambda, -1 + 2\lambda)$.

$(1 + 2\lambda) + 2(2 - \lambda) + 3(-1 + 2\lambda) = 2 + 6\lambda = 14 \Rightarrow \lambda = 2$.

Meeting point $(5, 0, 3)$.

**(b)** $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{n} = 2 - 2 + 6 = 6$, $|\vec{b}| = 3$, $|\vec{n}| = \sqrt{14}$: $\sin\phi = \dfrac{6}{3\sqrt{14}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{14}}$, so $\phi = \sin^{-1}\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{14}}$.

questions.solution_md: Line through two points meets the plane; sine formula.

questions.stem_md:
Two walls of an imagined art gallery lie in the planes $\pi_1: x - 2y + 2z = 3$ and $\pi_2: 6x + 2y + 3z = 7$, and a sculpture stands at $Q(1, 1, 1)$.

(a) Find the angle between the two walls. [2]

(b) Find the distance of $Q$ from each wall and say which wall is nearer. [2]

(c) Find the equation of the plane through $Q$ parallel to $\pi_1$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|6 - 4 + 6|}{3 \times 7} = \dfrac{8}{21}$, so $\theta = \cos^{-1}\dfrac{8}{21}$.

**(b)** From $\pi_1$: $\dfrac{|1 - 2 + 2 - 3|}{3} = \dfrac23$. From $\pi_2$: $\dfrac{|6 + 2 + 3 - 7|}{7} = \dfrac47$. Since $\dfrac47 < \dfrac23$, wall $\pi_2$ is nearer.

**(c)** $x - 2y + 2z = 1 - 2 + 2 = 1$.

questions.solution_md: Angle between normals; distance formula; same normal for a parallel plane.

questions.stem_md:
Three fixing points of an imagined solar panel are $A(1, 2, 3)$, $B(2, 0, 1)$ and $C(0, 1, 5)$.

(a) Find the equation of the plane of the panel. [2]

(b) Explain why the panel is parallel to the $y$-axis. [1]

(c) Write the plane in intercept form and name the axis it never meets. [1]

(d) Find the cosine of the angle between the panel and the ground $z = 0$. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\vec{AB} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$, $\vec{AC} = -\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$; $\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = -6\hat{i} - 3\hat{k}$, so $\vec{n} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{k}$ and $2x + z = 2 + 3 = 5$.

**(b)** The normal $2, 0, 1$ is perpendicular to $\hat{j}$ (dot product $0$), so the plane is parallel to the $y$-axis.

**(c)** $\dfrac{x}{5/2} + \dfrac{z}{5} = 1$; there is no $y$-term, so it never meets the $y$-axis.

**(d)** $\cos\theta = \dfrac{|1|}{\sqrt5 \times 1} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$.
